newsitem.title: UK: A year on, copper price bounces back from Sumitomo.
newsitem.headline: A year on, copper price bounces back from Sumitomo.

text.p: The world copper market has shown remarkable resilience since the Sumitomo debacle a year ago, recovering most of the ground lost in a crash amid revelations that the Japanese firm lost $2.6 billion in rogue trading.

"It's been a phenomenal performance. All credit to the copper price that it's clawed back to where it started," said analyst Robin Bhar of brokers Brandeis. "No-one would would have expected the tightness to have persisted," he added.
Analysts credit unexpected supply tightness for helping copper rebound nearly $1,000 from the lows of the past year.

On Thursday copper prices were trading at around $2,600 per tonne - actually firmer than on June 13, 1996, when Sumitomo Corp of Japan confirmed rumours of huge losses from what it called unauthorised trades.
Although analysts tend to agree prices will ease later this year as delayed production comes on stream, some caution that the market may not have felt the last of Sumitomo's legacy.

Copper started a dizzying downward spiral in mid-May 1996 from a cyclical high at $2,715 on rumours that Sumitomo's star copper trader Yasuo Hamanaka - widely suspected of squeezing the market by hoarding metal - had moved jobs.
Sumitomo's June 13 announcement that he had lost it hundreds of millions of dollars in unauthorised trading escalated the panic selling.
Within a month and a half, the price of copper had lost one-third of its value, bottoming out in late June at $1,745.
Since then, however unexpectedly strong world economic growth, supply hiccups in South and North America and other factors have kept prices climbing back up at a steady pace.
Scrap metal - or the absence of it at bargain-basement prices - also played a role in driving the copper market higher as end users were forced to buy primary metal to cover their needs.
In a recent Reuters survey of metal analysts, average copper prices for 1997 were revised up by most of those polled to an average of $2,293 per tonne.

"The fundamentals have been very supportive. Demand, especially in the U.S. market, has been stronger than people expected," said Angus Macmillian of Billiton. "Also production has not increased as fast as people believed."
The longer-term effect of Sumitomo on copper prices is difficult to gauge because the company has been tight-lipped about the volume of positions Hamanaka controlled.

Even as Hamanaka, 49, pleaded guilty to fraud and forgery charges at his continuing Tokyo trial, but denies manipulating the world market, Sumitomo has said it unwound his huge positions in copper futures - thereby ending that troubled chapter in its history.
But some analysts reckon that long-term and options positions were passed on to other brokers for managing - and are still occasionally tweaking the market as they are rolled forward.
The roll-on effect of former Sumitomo positions was blamed by some analysts for a supply squeeze as recently as April.
At that time, prices spiked by some $150 per tonne and the premium of cash over three months metal flared out to $200.
Post-Sumitomo blues may also have played a role in thinning copper trading on the LME over the past year.

"Copper turnover has still not recovered from the loss of confidence surrounding last year's Hamanaka debacle, with turnover down $15 on year-ago levels," analyst Nick Moore of Flemings Research said in a commentary.
Also since the scandal broke, two LME ring members have relinquished their seats on the floor - the latest being Deutsche Morgan Grenfell just this Wednesday.
From a broad market perspective, however, several important market factors have remained little changed.
London Metal Exchange (LME) stocks continue to be depleted, falling to seven-year lows at one point last November.
The market also remains stubbornly in backwardation, with the cash to three months spread at times expanding extravagantly to $300 over the past year.
"What's happening now, a year later, is some people are questioning whether Hamanaka actually did have such influence on the market that everyone pointed to," analyst Bhar said.
"Or is it an intrinsic factor of the copper market that it would have happened regardless whether Sumitomo manipulated the market or not?"
